b: I own a small gift shop and have one part-time employee, Ava. She’s one of the better I’ve had since few people want a job with so few hours and with really no room for advancement, but Ava is reliable and good with customers. Her job is mostly sales with a little light cleaning (sweeping, dusting, and arranging merchandise). We are friendly but not really friends.

The other day she had a run-in with a customer that I don’t know what to do about. Apparently a man walked in with a dog, and Ava told him that dogs weren’t allowed in the store. He told her this was a service dog and, on being told that service dogs weren’t allowed either, quickly became argumentative. He demanded to speak to her supervisor and, since I wasn’t around, she told him that was her. In no time he demanded her name, said he was calling the Department of Justice, and was generally aggressive. I wasn’t there, but I believe her when she says that he sounded threatening and belligerent because I heard his threatening tone when he complained on the store’s voicemail. He’s said he’s coming back — with his dog — and don’t try to keep him out.

I’ve looked into the law and see that it does seem to be the case that businesses aren’t allowed to deny entry to service dogs and they’re not even allowed to ask for proof that the dog is actually a service dog even if the dog pees on the floor or breaks merchandise. I’m mildly allergic to dogs (might make me sneeze but won’t send me to the hospital). Ava says she’s not only allergic to dogs but also afraid of them, phobic, panic attack territory. I didn’t know any of this because it’s not the sort of thing that comes up on a job application for a part-time sales position for a job that doesn’t cater to pets. She could be making it up, but I don’t think so. She has no track record of lying.

What do I do now? Ava alternates between saying she has a disability (her allergy and phobia) so I have to guarantee her a dog-free workspace and saying she’ll quit if she has to allow dogs in the store. The customer has said he has the right to bring his dog anywhere he wants. I don’t want to lose my good employee. I also can’t afford to be sued by a man who seems determined to bring his dog in the store to prove a point.
First, I’m not a lawyer and you should consider consulting one! With that caveat in place…

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) does indeed require businesses to allow service dogs to enter. And it’s true that you can’t demand proof that the dog is indeed a service dog. You’re allowed to ask whether the dog is a service animal required because of a disability, and what work or task the dog has been trained to perform. You’re not allowed to ask about the customer’s specific disability, demand documentation, or ask the dog to demonstrate the task.

However, it’s not correct that you’d need to permit a dog who was peeing on the floor or destroying merchandise. The law requires that you allow a service dog entry, but also requires that the dog remain under the handler’s control. If that’s not happening, you have the right to ask the customer to remove the dog from the store.

The customer also doesn’t have the right to harass or threaten your staff — although I can understand why he was upset because Ava flat-out misstated the law to him when she said service dogs weren’t allowed in. That’s a training issue that you’ve got to remedy with Ava.

On Ava’s side of things, it’s not really true that you have to guarantee her a dog-free workspace. If you were a larger business, the ADA would require you to provide her with medical accommodations (which could mean ensuring she’s not around dogs), but the ADA only covers employers with at least 15 employees. It’s possible that your state has a law that kicks in at a lower number of employees and you should check to be sure, but very few apply to a business with just two people. Even if it did cover you, though, it wouldn’t mean you had to (or even could) deny entry to service dogs; it would mean you needed to come up with an accommodation for her (like letting her go in a back room while a dog was in the store, if that could be done without undue hardship to the business).

But the law aside, Ava is a good worker and you want to keep her so you should look for compromises that meet her needs without violating the customer’s rights. For example, can you give her permission to immediately move to a back room as soon as a service dog enters the store? This is tricky since it sounds like she’s often working by herself, but could she call you and could you then get there fast enough to handle the customer’s check-out yourself?

If that’s not practical — and I’m guessing it probably isn’t, at least not 100% of the time — then you’ve got to have a conversation with Ava where you explain that you can’t guarantee she’ll never be around a service dog because the law does require you to allow them in the store, and say you want to talk about whether there are arrangements that will help her feel safer. Then ask her to brainstorm with you. Can she step away while the customer shops but return briefly to check him out? Is there a check-out set-up that could provide more distance? Is there some other arrangement that she thinks would make solo shifts manageable?

If there’s no arrangement she’d be comfortable with, it might be that she’s simply not able to work a solo shift in a retail shop that’s open to the public. But try to genuinely explore alternatives with her before either of you conclude that.

One other thought: you can’t require the customer to make an appointment for a time when you’ll be there (the law requires people with disabilities to receive the same spontaneous, walk-in access to retail stores as any other customer), but you could offer him that. You could call him back and say something like, “I want to clarify that service animals are welcome in our store in compliance with the ADA. My employee was mistaken about our policy, and I have since corrected that. Because we’re a very small shop and have a staff member with severe dog allergies, I want to ensure your next visit is seamless. While you are welcome at any time, if you’re open to letting me know when you plan to stop by, I will gladly make sure I am there to assist you.”

But that doesn’t solve the larger issue, which is that a totally different customer with a service dog could walk in tomorrow, and you and Ava need to have a plan for (legally) handling that if it happens.
